The most specific incident was a Message Authentication Code (MAC) layer failure. That layer let corporate users validate payment integrity before release. The account does not specify the incident’s duration, the number of affected payments, or the precise code fix.

There were also **post-cutover data issues carried over from the legacy platform during migration**. Regional systems had different schemas, client configurations, entitlement structures, and transaction histories. Matt ran UAT and production validation/shakeout testing and triaged the defects that emerged after cutover. Those defects should not be confused with a payment-processing outage: the migration was completed **without disruption to live payment operations**.

Across successive releases, waves, and migrations, Matt repeatedly owned **Sev-1 incident response** and on-call accountability. He coordinated root-cause analysis across New York, Mumbai, Bangalore, and the Bottomline Technologies vendor team, while running status updates and daily leadership calls during live issues.

The underlying delivery constraint was that WebSeries’ out-of-box capabilities did not cover the bank’s payment, security, and workflow requirements. Matt managed where platform configuration ended and bespoke engineering began under aggressive delivery timelines. Matt owned the daily ETL between shop-floor material tracking and the master configuration system. Later, at **Accenture**, he led Project Octane: reusable reference applications, automated infrastructure provisioning, and hands-on workshops for engineers adopting cloud-native technologies. The reference applications included real-time GraphQL sync using AWS AppSync, backed by ElastiCache, with infrastructure as code for each stack.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt describes his leadership.

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. At **Accenture**, he inherited engineering teams that were “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” In the early Cloud Innovation Center, a rigid hierarchy made people slow to share ideas. Fear of blame also kept teams from experimenting, contributing to slower delivery and missed opportunities.

He made intent explicit and pushed decisions to the people closest to the work. He used transparency, direct feedback, and open communication, and coached teams to think clearly rather than just execute tasks. Weekly brainstorming sessions gave people space to contribute ideas without judgment. He emphasized shared goals over individual accolades and recognized contributions that advanced the team’s mission.

His “permit to fail” culture included non-punitive post-mortems and lean, low-stakes experiments. In product incubation, he set expectations upfront that prototypes and user tests would likely fail. Teams used user research, rapid testing, and the build-measure-learn loop to test assumptions before committing to costly builds. Failed experiments became decision inputs, not occasions for blame.

He also brought product managers, designers, and engineers together in balanced teams. They prioritized essential features and delivered thin-slice, production-ready solutions for rapid user feedback, supported by automation, continuous delivery, and quality-first practices.

At the Cloud Innovation Center, teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** after adopting lean product and modern engineering practices. Post-mortem lessons prevented recurrence of identified failure patterns, and client teams continued using iterative delivery practices after engagements ended.

answer_md:
🐾 Yes. Matt describes a delivery failure where he relied on assumptions instead of verifying the environment his team was working in.

He was the tech lead on a global platform modernization for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams running test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. IAM controls, environment boundaries, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from earlier phases.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. Instead, he relied on inherited documentation without confirming its accuracy. He did not audit who could trigger downstream email jobs, implement email interception, or verify that production customer names and email addresses had been masked in downstream environments.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. Communications containing unmasked production customer data went to **thousands of real clients**. This was not a controlled, low-stakes experiment.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. But the client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt describes it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” His commitment to learning without blame did not prevent that consequence.

Afterward, Matt made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach. His own description of the failure is direct: these were “assumptions I should have verified rather than inherited.”

Matt worked to remove those barriers rather than add more process. He made intent explicit, pushed decisions to the people closest to the work, and used transparency, direct feedback, and open communication. He coached teams to think clearly, not just execute tasks.

He used user research, Jobs to Be Done framing, and rapid testing to challenge assumptions before committing to costly builds. Failed experiments became decision inputs that shaped product direction week by week.

He also brought product managers, designers, and engineers together in balanced teams. They delivered thin-slice, production-ready solutions for rapid user feedback, supported by automation, continuous delivery, and quality-first engineering practices.

At the Cloud Innovation Center, teams accelerated delivery **4x** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices. In the “permit to fail” work, teams experimented more freely, repeat errors declined, and delivery timelines shortened.

The pilot maintained full HIPAA compliance. Clinical teams adopted AI-generated insights into treatment planning, and the executive team approved consideration of broader AI implementation.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a time Matt failed.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup, but he relied on that documentation rather than verifying it. He assumed the IAM configuration and environment boundaries were correct. He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, implement compensating controls such as data masking and email interception, or verify that production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. Rather than treating the tester’s action as the whole explanation, the team examined insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed. They worked collectively to understand what happened and implement corrective controls.

The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” His stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise.” IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production environments. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

His responsibility was to ensure a safe environment setup. Instead, he relied on that documentation without confirming its accuracy. He did not verify who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, confirm that production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed, or implement compensating controls such as data masking and email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. He worked collectively with the team to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. The root causes were insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments.

The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.”

His stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise.” Afterward, he made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s Matt’s payments work, from payment-engine delivery to cross-border workflow design and developer integration.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, ACCESS Next Generation needed capabilities well beyond Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform. Different payment types had distinct formatting, validation, compliance, and workflow requirements, serving **135,000+ clients** across **180+ countries**. Regional legacy systems also had different data models, entitlements, and transaction histories that had to be consolidated without interrupting live payments.

As Technology Delivery Lead, Matt managed a blended team of **40+** across **Accenture** and **JP Morgan Chase**, working across Mumbai, Bangalore, and the US. He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and federal tax payment modules. His work included NACHA file validation, Message Authentication Code security, payment-type-specific entitlements, sanctions screening, and risk-based approval controls. He also led payments data migration, introduced compliance dashboards, and owned production incident response. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**; the migration completed **without disruption to live payment operations**, with compliance traceability maintained.

At **RBC**, fragmented systems and manual processes were delaying cross-border payments and bulk processing. Matt designed workflows from initiation through settlement and reconciliation, partnering with the FX team on real-time currency conversion and transaction visibility. He also designed recurring payments, Interac e-Transfer workflows, and batch processing. The work produced a complete implementation blueprint; revised payment cutoff processes reduced wire-transfer delays and improved SLA compliance.

At **American Express**, Virtual Payments Platform adoption was slowed by missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, no sandbox, and testing dependencies. Matt led developer-portal work that added Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, use-case-driven documentation, a secure sandbox, and virtualized testing environments. His team used Lean Product and XP practices and validated the experience through a Client Onboarding Test Drive. API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch, onboarding time fell, and the team delivered **over 261 additional story points** beyond its commitment.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt describes his leadership: empathy, clarity, and purpose.

Many engineering teams he inherited were “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” In the early Cloud Innovation Center, a rigid hierarchical culture left people slow to share ideas. Teams also avoided risks because they feared blame, which slowed delivery and experimentation.

Matt pushed decisions to the people closest to the work, made intent explicit, and used transparency and direct feedback. He established weekly brainstorming sessions where ideas were considered without judgment. Instead of emphasizing individual accolades, he recognized contributions that advanced shared project goals.

He also established a “permit to fail” environment. That meant non-punitive post-mortems, transparent discussion of mistakes, and low-stakes experiments with structured hypotheses. Teams applied lessons from post-mortems in subsequent sprints to prevent recurring errors. In early product work, he set expectations that prototypes and user tests would sometimes fail intentionally: the goal was to test assumptions before committing to costly builds, then adjust product direction week by week.

His day-to-day working model brought product managers, designers, and engineers together in balanced teams. He coached teams to think clearly, not just execute tasks, and grounded delivery in automation, continuous delivery, and quality-first practices. Teams delivered thin-slice, production-ready solutions so user feedback could inform the next iteration.

At **Accenture’s** **150-person** Cloud Innovation Center, teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** once they embraced lean product and modern engineering practices. The change took time; teams also began experimenting more freely, repeat errors declined, and delivery timelines shortened.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s an example from **Norfolk Southern**.

In early **2020**, Matt’s Cloud Innovation Center team was modernizing the client’s Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A couple of months into the engagement, as the pandemic forced work remote, the client reported rising defects. The team’s dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The concerns landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery.

Matt took ownership of the failure in front of both groups rather than defending the metrics. He led a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and shared the gaps openly. An engineer had been working from his own interpretation rather than the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. The backlog also lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done, leaving no clear way to test the requirements.

Matt addressed both the engineering practices and the conditions around them. He rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought in frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work alongside the team. Engineers redid the code and test cases, supported by boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, and pairing with subject-matter experts using an “I do, we do, you do” progression.

He also restructured agile ceremonies to keep stakeholders, developers, and product managers aligned, with product-management and SMART-story training to address the gaps exposed by the audit.

Defect rates dropped, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Client and account-leadership confidence was restored through the open audit and visible improvement.

🐾 Here’s a specific example from **Norfolk Southern**.

In **2020**, Matt’s team was modernizing the railroad’s legacy Revenue and Shipment Planning platform when the client reported rising defects. The dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. Matt took ownership of the failure rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and shared the gaps openly. An engineer had been building from his own interpretation rather than the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. The backlog was also part of the problem: stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done, leaving engineers without clear requirements to test against.

Instead of simply telling the team to follow the process, Matt rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought in frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work alongside the engineers. They redid the code and test cases, using boot camps, coding katas, and an “I do, we do, you do” coaching progression.

He then reinforced the practices after the experts left. New engineers paired with seasoned practitioners, pairs rotated daily to spread knowledge, and test cases became a visible step before implementation. During remote work, pairs traded drivers frequently to reduce fatigue and break mental blocks.

The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. **The original failure mode did not recur**, and knowledge stopped bottlenecking on individual engineers. Pairing and test-first remained the team’s default after the outside experts went home.

🐾 Matt’s payments work includes building global payment infrastructure at **JP Morgan Chase** and reducing integration barriers for **American Express’s** Virtual Payments Platform.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, regional payment systems had different data models, entitlement structures, message formats, and regulatory requirements. Matt co-created a developer portal with Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, sample integrations, use case-driven documentation, and a secure sandbox with refreshed client data. He introduced environment virtualization, Lean Product and XP practices, and a Client Onboarding Test Drive.

🐾 Here’s how Matt describes leading teams.

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. He describes teams he inherited as “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center, a rigid hierarchical culture made people slow to share ideas, while fear of blame discouraged experimentation and slowed delivery.

He worked to remove those barriers rather than add more process. Matt made intent explicit, pushed decisions to the people closest to the work, and used transparency, direct feedback, and open communication. He coached teams to think clearly, not just execute tasks. He brought product managers, designers, and engineers together in balanced teams, prioritizing essential features and delivering thin-slice, production-ready solutions for rapid user feedback.

His “permit to fail” approach included non-punitive post-mortems, transparent discussion of mistakes, and lean, low-stakes experiments with structured hypotheses and controlled iterations. In early-stage product work, he set expectations that prototypes and user tests would likely fail. Teams used user research, Jobs to Be Done framing, and rapid testing to challenge assumptions before committing to costly builds.

Matt also established weekly brainstorming sessions where ideas were considered without judgment. He emphasized shared goals over individual accolades and recognized contributions that advanced the team’s mission.

At the Cloud Innovation Center, teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices. Teams applied post-mortem lessons in subsequent sprints, preventing recurrence of identified failure patterns, and used early experiments to eliminate wrong directions before further engineering investment.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s an example from **Norfolk Southern**.

In early **2020**, Matt’s Cloud Innovation Center team was modernizing the client’s legacy Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A couple of months into the engagement, the client reported rising defects, even though the dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The concerns landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, just as the pandemic forced the team into remote work.

Matt took ownership of the failure rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and shared the gaps openly. An engineer had been building from his own interpretation instead of the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. Coverage looked complete, but defects went undetected. The backlog was also part of the problem: stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done.

Instead of treating it solely as an individual performance issue or adding another process checkpoint, Matt rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought in frontend and backend test-driven development experts from Columbus. They worked side by side with the team and redid the code and test cases properly.

He used the Samman coaching approach: boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, and pairing engineers with subject-matter experts through an “I do, we do, you do” progression. He also restructured agile ceremonies and provided product management and SMART story training.

Defect rates dropped as story quality and test-first discipline took hold. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see, and confidence was restored through the open audit and visible improvements.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s the story of Matt’s **Norfolk Southern** work.

As a Director at **Accenture**, Matt led modernization of the railroad’s Revenue and Shipment Planning systems from **November 2019 to September 2023**, the Cloud Innovation Center’s first engagement. Core scheduling, billing, and order-to-cash ran on a mainframe dating to the **1970s**. Orders could fall out unnoticed until customers called, business rules lived in COBOL and assembly maintained by a shrinking workforce, and clerks manually resolved waybill and rating problems. The work also faced resistance from a client organization accustomed to mainframes and account leadership accustomed to waterfall, while his own team learned a new working model during COVID.

Matt led domain-driven design and event storming sessions to map business functions and dependencies. Rather than attempt a wholesale replacement, his team kept the mainframe as the system of record while building APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB alongside it. Change data capture synchronized the platforms, and reconciliation reports checked that no functionality or data was lost. Docker, Kubernetes, automated CI/CD, and TDD supported incremental replacement on live production.

When the client grew restless for tangible progress, Matt brought its revenue management team into the innovation hub to co-create the Shipper Revenue System workspace. They worked through personas, user flows, and prototypes in weekly build-measure-learn iterations. He also led a **2-day** CIC Academy course delivered twice monthly over **6 months**. Pairing helped spread scarce legacy knowledge and gave client contributors experience with Angular, Node, Spring Boot, and cloud-native development.

The MVP launched covering **95% of its targeted use cases**, capturing real orders with clean data feeding the mainframe. EDI validation moved fallout detection from customer complaints to proactive trading-partner notifications. Delivery scaled to **3 balanced teams**, and the client took ownership of its backlog and priorities while learning to support and manage the new application.

answer_md:
🐾 Let’s dig into the quality crisis within that **Norfolk Southern** engagement.

A few months into the Cloud Innovation Center’s first engagement, the client reported rising defects even though the team’s dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The pandemic had just pushed everyone into remote work. Engineers were learning a new delivery model, and the client and **Accenture** account leadership were already accustomed to waterfall delivery. The defect reports put the team’s work under scrutiny while they were modernizing a live Revenue and Shipment Planning platform.

Matt took ownership in front of the client and account leadership rather than defending the coverage metrics. A bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite exposed the mismatch: an engineer was building from his own interpretation instead of the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. Coverage looked complete, but the tests were not catching departures from the requirements. The backlog contributed to the problem: stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done.

Matt showed those gaps openly and rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories. He brought frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work alongside the engineers, demonstrating test-first development while redoing the code and test cases.

The coaching continued through boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, and lunch and learns. Engineers paired with subject-matter experts through an “I do, we do, you do” progression. Product managers received product management and SMART story training, while restructured agile ceremonies kept developers, product managers, and stakeholders working from the same requirements.

Defect rates dropped as story quality and test-first discipline took hold. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Engineers had defined scenarios to implement and test, and client and account leadership confidence returned through the open audit and visible improvement.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt built and ran that organization.

The CIC stories describe growth from a **10-person pilot to 150+ practitioners**, rather than a starting team of **4**. At **Accenture**, Matt built the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers as client demand grew. Many new hires lacked hands-on cloud-native or Agile experience. The organization also needed ways to hire, develop, and evaluate people without adding traditional management layers.

Matt built a hiring engine across bench search, campus recruiting, contract-to-hire, and approved job requisitions. Instead of relying only on interviews, engineers completed hands-on TDD pairing auditions; product managers and designers worked through live scoping exercises. Interviewers recorded independent votes, and Matt held the closing interview and made every final hiring decision. During scaling pushes, the process added **4 to 6 net-new practitioners per week**, with interview participation capped at **2 slots per practitioner per week** to protect delivery.

New joiners moved through structured enablement and round-robin pairing with seasoned practitioners. The learning model was “I do, we do, you do,” progressing from guided to independent delivery. Skills matrices, senior-junior mentoring, peer-led demos, and learning inside live client projects supported continued development.

Matt kept the organization deliberately flat: **11 to 13 practice and client leads** reported directly to him. Balanced teams combined engineering, product, and design, with experienced engineering anchors inside teams rather than another management layer. Monday allocation reviews matched practitioners to engagements and internal learning work. Because managers did not sit on daily teams, evaluations drew on evidence from recent pair partners, product managers, and anchors, rather than visibility to the boss.

The organization reached **150+ practitioners**, with **near-zero attrition in the first 2 years** and multiple hires promoted. Across the CIC delivery model, **10-person balanced teams** delivered equivalent output to traditional **20-person teams**, with **4X faster velocity** and **zero-defect deployments**.

🐾 Matt’s payments work includes building the payment engine behind **JP Morgan Chase** ACCESS and improving adoption of **American Express**’s Virtual Payments Platform.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, regional payment systems had different formats, protocols, client configurations, and compliance records. Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform provided the foundation for ACCESS, but the bank needed purpose-built capabilities for **135,000+ clients** across **180+ countries**.

As Technology Delivery Lead, Matt managed a blended **40+ person** **Accenture** and bank team across the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore. He defined the onshore-offshore engagement model and spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded with Bottomline in Portsmouth, coordinating with bank teams in Chicago and NY/NJ. He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and tax payment modules, alongside payment verification, payment-type-specific permissions, sanctions screening, and risk-based approval controls.

He also designed the centralized gateway connecting ACCESS to payment rails across **12 countries**, handling message transformation, protocol translation, and routing. For the legacy migration, he coordinated data verification with compliance teams, introduced compliance dashboards, and owned production validation and defect triage. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**; the migration completed **without disruption to live payment operations**. Matt also directed critical production incident response, cross-team root-cause analysis, and daily leadership calls.

At **American Express**, the challenge was adoption: missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, no sandbox, and delayed testing made the Virtual Payments Platform difficult to evaluate and integrate. Matt brought business and technical teams together through Discovery and Framing workshops, then led work on the developer portal, Java/.NET/Python SDKs, use-case-driven documentation, and secure virtualized testing environments. A Client Onboarding Test Drive gathered end-user feedback.

API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch, onboarding time decreased, and the portal team delivered **over 261 additional story points** beyond its delivery commitment.

answer_md:
🐾 Found it! Matt was brought in roughly seven months into **Fiserv**'s 14-month, **$8.5M** white-label card portal program, the shared platform behind branded credit card sites for **2M+** cardholders across **15** financial institutions. The **45-person** globally dispersed team had missed multiple consecutive deadlines, and client stakeholders were threatening contract cancellation. He recovered a Q4 release that was **3 weeks** behind, avoiding **$500K** in penalties, and the program was delivered **3%** under budget with zero critical defects at launch.

Want to hear how he moved that team from 6-month waterfall releases to 2-week sprints?

🐾 Here’s how Matt changed the day-to-day work.

At **Fiserv**, the **45-person** team was working in **6-month** waterfall release cycles, with requirements buried in a **200-page** BRD organized by system modules. Developers in India, testers in the Philippines, and designers in Ireland had no shared visibility into work status. Deadlines kept slipping, and client stakeholders were threatening contract cancellation. PMO and compliance also resisted the move to agile, while some stakeholders lacked bandwidth for feedback every **2 weeks**.

Matt changed how the work was defined and tracked, rather than just adding sprint meetings. He decomposed the BRD into persona-based user stories and replaced a single To Do/Done JIRA board with a multi-tiered Kanban/Scrum architecture. The **47** acceptance criteria became Epics, with user stories moving through specific workflow columns.

He established **7 AM CST** scrum-of-scrums for offshore-to-onshore handoffs and **11 PM CST** syncs for the reverse handoff. Sprint demos every **2 weeks** brought branding, UI, and ADA compliance decisions forward instead of leaving them until month **6**. He negotiated dedicated review windows and maintained existing steering committee reporting while adding sprint-level visibility.

For compliance, Matt used JIRA as the system of record, with audit trails, attached ADA scans, and developer comments instead of static Word documents. He also trained offshore teams on screen reader audits using JAWS/NVDA and made those audits part of the Definition of Done.

The team reached a **2-week** sprint cadence within **3 months**. JIRA gave **50+** stakeholders across **3** time zones real-time visibility, and PMO and compliance accepted it for audit requirements. Separately, production deployments increased from less than once per month to weekly-to-monthly cycles, not necessarily every sprint.

The MVP launched covering **95%** of its targeted use cases, capturing real orders with clean data feeding the mainframe. EDI validation moved fallout detection from customer complaints to proactive trading-partner notifications.
